No, Li-ion batteries are far more volatile than you think.

Damage any Li-ion battery, and it will very likely start reacting violently. If it is damaged internally, but the shell is intact, it is likely to explode. If the shell is ruptured, a runaway exothermic reaction creates immense heat, flames and toxic fumes. Many Li-ion batteries have vents, specifically to prevent explosion if it comes to this (but then you still get flames and fumes coming from those vents instead). Even just overcharging the battery can cause it to go off like this. Which is why most Li-ion batteries have built-in electronics to prevent overcharging. Tesla ones don't, instead opting for a centralized charging logic solution.

Voat has been attacked via DDOS two times now by professionals. They are professionals because both the scale and methods employed are nothing less than professional. The first attack of this caliber used website end-points that were expensive and not widely known (a normal user seldom navigates to these areas of the website). In response we made changes and discontinued publishing code to our github repo. This was a defensive move. This latest attack was responsive in that they were monitoring Voat. When I turned Voat off, they stopped sending traffic, but within minutes of enabling Voat, they continued their assault.

In response to this dynamic nature, the only thing I could do was to prevent the botnet from being able to function how it was. I accomplished this by requiring Authorized Only access as typical DDOS attacks on a smaller site like Voat don’t usually come with advanced planning (e.g. creating accounts). This is something I've been wondering for a while. When a website is targeted for attack by a botnet, why doesn't the subject of the attack harvest the IPs of the attackers and contact the ISPs of the infected machines e.g., this article which mentions Comcast's pledge to contact infected hosts?

This would give the owners of infected machines an opportunity to sanitize their devices.

Obviously there are some issues with this:

* Source ISPs might be operating out of countries that couldn't care less (I'm looking at you China)

* ISPs seem reluctant to enforce a "walled garden" approach to infected users, so if a user doesn't do anything about their infected host, nothing will come of being notified about it

* Infected users might be technically incapable of removing infections

* Infected users might be financially incapable of upgrading their way out of infection (i.e., stuck on Windows XP)

* ISPs might not trust the persons reporting attacks (i.e., it might be assumed that hostile parties will report hosts for disingenuous reasons, disenfranchised former customers, competitors... ticked off gamers annoyed that someone outscored them on CounterStrike)

* Users might refuse to acknowledge fault

I'm sure you can think of others. But it's odd to me that there isn't more coordination worldwide to cut down on infected hosts spewing nefarious traffic online. Obviously this is another regulation vs freedom issue (in other words, should ISP have the power to block clients on the basis of harmful traffic, a power that could be abused), and yet...
Why don't attack targets contact attacker ISPs in the case of a DDOS?

"Distributed" is the biggie... These attacks come from a botnet that consists of a LOT of compromised machines. Tens of thousands, hundreds of thousands, or even millions of PCs making calls to the same website from all over the world.
Yeah, you're right, it would be a bit of a nightmare to coordinate a fightback. But I'm surprised there isn't software to automate this process. Or perhaps there is, but it hasn't proven effective?

Yes and no. You can do a lot with routers. The big problem is that these attacks come across as normal web traffic. For instance during the now-infamous Voat attack of 2019 the botnet was calling the Junkerman /pizzagate thread over and over and over from thousands and thousands of machines. That's why a service like Cloudflare is effective at preventing a DDOS attack. When you replicate your site across a Content Delivery Network, there is no longer a single machine to attack. I digress... The problem you find with creating new routing rules on your firewall is the inevitability of blocking legitimate traffic at the same time.

You would need to do this at the firewall level. While this could be done at the router level, the amount of inbound traffic would overwhelm most routers' ram if it had to do any type of packet inspection on everything inbound.

Firewalls allow a little more flexibility. The real problem is yes, you could write a dynamic rule to block all inbound traffic the behaves a certain way (such as a bot), but once the attacker(s) realize they are being blocked, they will change their method of attack to bypass the firewall rule and now the site owner has to collect new traffic signatures from the new attack and deploy new signatures. It's like a game of whack--a-mole.

What I have done in the past is setup a mirror of my main site on a different server/network and I keep that info private. Whenever I would get a valid attack, I would redirect the traffic to the different server/network so it can take the brunt of the bad traffic while leaving the real site functioning. That also provides a bit of forensic evidence in that the traffic logs from the "secret" server would be filled with just the IP addresses of these bad actors.
